added_provisions.reason: Section 32(1)(a) as substituted requires the caveat to be 'substantially in Form VIII of the Second Schedule', and the gold conclusion turns on lodging in Form VIII, but no provision carried the Form. Section 5(1) of Act No. 32 of 2022 substitutes it. The substituted Form is also the direct authority for the notary limb of CL-M015-Q01-013, which otherwise rested only on section 26(1)(d).

Section 32(1A), inserted by section 2(2) of the 2022 Act, is the step that makes the paragraph (b) conditions operative: the Registrar acknowledges the caveat only on being satisfied that all the required documents and information are provided. The map relied on this in CL-M015-Q01-010 and in the counterfactual for FACT-M015-Q01-002 without citing it.

CL-M015-Q01-008 asserts a sixty-day window running from the posting of the notice. PROV-M015-010 carries only the amending directive and PROV-M015-009 only subsection (2), so the host subsection 32(5) supplying the trigger, the running point and the relief was uncited.

question_decisions.note: Kept as proposed_gold: no indispensable provision was rejected or left unresolved, and every rule, application and conclusion claim is carried by statutory text. Both limbs are decided on the face of section 32 as substituted; no Roman-Dutch principle or decided case is needed, and none is cited. Hop count stays at 3; the four added provisions sit on the existing third step. One claim, CL-M015-Q01-013, is marked disputed on the narrow ground that the notary's authority to present a caveat rests on Form VIII rather than on section 26(1)(d).

disagreements.researcher_position: Section 26(1)(d) of the Ordinance confirms that a notary may present a caveat for registration on behalf of an entitled person.
disagreements.verifier_position: Section 26 governs presentation of an 'instrument', and section 25 defines 'instrument' for that Chapter as 'an instrument affecting land or a pledge, mortgage or bill of sale'. A caveat is not obviously within that definition, although section 32(2) directs that a caveat be registered 'in the same manner as other instruments'. The safer authority is substituted Form VIII, whose signature line reads '(Signature of the caveator/his Attorney-at-Law or notary/attorney)'. Section 26(1)(d) has been demoted to supporting and Form VIII added.

disagreements.researcher_position: Recorded as a corpus gap: commencement is inferred from the enactment year because section 1 of the Act gives only a short title.
disagreements.verifier_position: The absence of an appointed-date provision is itself the answer on the corpus text. Section 1 of the 2022 Act contains no commencement clause, in contrast to section 1(2) of Act No. 18 of 2024, which postpones operation to a date the Minister appoints by Gazette Order. The 2022 Act therefore operated on certification in 2022 and was in force at 2025-10. Recorded as an added corpus_gaps entry rather than a block.

disagreements.researcher_position: matter_reference_date_basis states that Act No. 18 of 2024 'is in force but does not touch section 32'.
disagreements.verifier_position: It certainly does not touch section 32; its toc shows amendments to sections 8, 25, 29, 41, Chapter IV and the First Schedule only. But its section 1(2) makes operation depend on an appointed date the corpus does not carry, so 'is in force' is stated more firmly than the corpus supports. Immaterial to this answer, since nothing here depends on the 2024 Act.

Not added, but noted: section 34 of the Ordinance makes a person who registers a caveat without reasonable cause liable to compensate anyone injured. The counterfactual to FACT-M015-Q01-005 relies on exactly this and cites no provision. It is advice-side rather than part of the standing test, so it was left out; a lawyer may want it in the gold answer.

Not added: section 33(2A) inserted by the 2022 Act directs that summons, notices and orders in caveat proceedings go to the caveator's Sri Lanka address under section 32(1)(b)(iv). It reinforces the map's central point about a departing caveator and could be added if the lawyer wants that emphasis.
Not added: the fee item in section 5 of Act No. 21 of 2013 (2,500 rupees per land per two-year period). Agreed with the researcher that it goes to cost, not to standing.
case_law_dependence: None. No claim in the map cites or needs a decided case, and no Roman-Dutch doctrine is engaged: the question is entirely about the text of an amended statutory provision.
enrichment_issues: FACT-M015-Q01-002 is labelled synthetic_neutral, but its own reason and counterfactual say the caveat 'would not be accepted' without it. On the map's own definition that is decisive, not neutral. Same tension, less acutely, in FACT-M015-Q01-004, whose counterfactual says an unregistered power of attorney could not supply the required certified copy.

Facts 002 and 003 track the statutory checklist so closely (in duplicate, affidavit, attorney-at-law's certificate, an address in Sri Lanka for service) that a candidate could recite most of section 32(1)(b) straight out of the fact pattern. No statute name, section number or conclusion is leaked, so this is not a hard leak, but it lowers the difficulty of the applied limb. Worth a lawyer's eye on whether to soften the wording.

lawyer_questions: Most important: is it acceptable for a gold answer to state the operative text of section 32 by quoting the amending sections of Act No. 32 of 2022, given that the corpus holds only the 1990 consolidation and no consolidated post-2022 section 32 exists? Every operative claim in this matter depends on that method.

May a notary present a caveat for registration under section 26(1)(d), given that section 25 defines 'instrument' for that Chapter as an instrument affecting land or a pledge, mortgage or bill of sale, and that section 32(2) speaks of registering a caveat 'in the same manner as other instruments'? Substituted Form VIII names the notary as a signatory, which may be the better route.
Should the gold answer mention section 34 (compensation for registering a caveat without reasonable cause) as part of the advice to a client lodging a caveat before leaving the country?

Is a caveat renewable at all under section 32(3) as substituted ('a maximum period of two years'), or must a fresh caveat be lodged? The gold answer says the caveat 'will have to be renewed' during a three-year absence, and the corpus does not carry a renewal provision for caveats specifically; section 34 and section 44 use the language of renewal, and the fee item in Act No. 21 of 2013 is expressed per two-year period.
Should FACT-M015-Q01-002 be re-labelled synthetic_decisive, and should facts 002 and 003 be reworded so that they do not recite the section 32(1)(b) checklist back to the candidate?
